spans.t: This is a small book for nine days. It is made to go with the Camino Portugués Costero, the coastal route from Porto to Santiago de Compostela, which the CaminoPlus catalogue gives as ~260 km. That figure is approximate, so check the current route before you go. Read one day for each day of walking, or one for each day at home. If your road is longer, rest a day or read a day twice. If it is shorter, read two on a long evening.
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from
St. Francis of Assisi
, a short life of the saint by the English writer G. K. Chesterton. The words are exactly his, in the English he wrote.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Chesterton's. It starts from something on the road, a boardwalk, a gull, a pack, and lets the passage open it. It says plainly what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back over the day you have just lived, with the morning's passage in mind. It asks two or three gentle questions and is honest about tiredness.
A short prayer.
If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish, to nobody in particular.

spans.t: Why this book for this road
Three things in Chesterton's Francis seem to belong on a coast.

The first is creation. He calls the sun, the moon, fire and water his brothers and sisters, and sings about them. The route guide in the app describes dunes, fishing villages and long boardwalks on this road, with wind and sun as its main challenge.

The second is the sea. Francis sets out across it twice in Chesterton's story, and the first time he goes as a stowaway, boarding a ship without waiting for arrangements. A road beside the Atlantic suits him.

The third is joy and poverty, which Chesterton insists belong together. A pack, a bunk and a plain supper are a small, chosen version of the way Francis lived. They are not the same thing, and the book says so. But a walker who has lived out of one pack for a week has a taste of what Chesterton means by travelling light.
A Christian saint and a Catholic writer

Francis is a saint of the Catholic Church, and Chesterton wrote as a believer, for readers who admired Francis but found much of him hard to follow. This is a Christian book, and we say so plainly. People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Chesterton believed to notice what he noticed about gratitude, courtesy and travelling light.
It is also his portrait, not Francis's own words, and a book of its time. The next chapter says what that means, and a day says so briefly when it comes close.
The shape of the nine days
The days follow Francis's life in the order Chesterton tells it, from the young man to his death.

items.t: Day 1, the boast and the turning back.
The young man of Assisi.
Day 2, everything that can be called his.
The break with his father.
Day 3, expecting nothing, enjoying everything.
Where his joy came from.
Day 4, a stranger on the road.
The poor man as others saw him.
Day 5, Brother Fire, Sister Water.
The creatures and the song of the sun.
Day 6, nothing to hold him by.
The brothers and their rule.
Day 7, what may never be known.
The journey East, and Alverno.
Day 8, the bare ground.
His death.
Day 9, always going home.
What he left, and how to go on.

spans.t: The days are a shape, not a timetable. Read the one that fits the day you are having. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer, and leave the rest.
On the road and at home
Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk in an
albergue

(the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep), or at a café table while the soup arrives. Take the question with you for an hour. Read the evening part last, when the boots are off. At home, use your tea and your bedtime.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly
may your Way go well
. On the Portuguese side you may hear
Bom caminho
, which means the same.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The saint

Francis of Assisi lived from about 1181 to 1226. The edition we use gives no dates, only that he was not fifty when he died, so these are the well-known ones, and the first is approximate. He was born in Assisi, a walled town on the hills of Umbria, in central Italy, the son of a cloth merchant. As a young man he gave up the merchant's life, took to the roads in a rough brown tunic tied with a rope, and gathered a band of followers that came to be called the Friars Minor, or, as Chesterton prefers, the Little Brothers. He is a saint of the Catholic Church. He left some writings of his own, among them his song in praise of the creatures. This book is not one of them.
The author

Gilbert Keith Chesterton lived from 1874 to 1936. He was an English journalist, novelist, poet and Christian apologist, which means a writer who defends his faith in argument. He is best known for the Father Brown stories, about a priest who solves crimes, and for a great many essays, written quickly and with a love of paradox. He became a Catholic in 1922, and
St. Francis of Assisi
came out the following year. These dates are general knowledge, and the edition we used does not state them.
The book
The book is a short life of Francis, about 44,000 words by our count, in ten chapters. One of the chapter titles is French,
Le Jongleur de Dieu
, which means the minstrel and jester of God.

Chesterton tells you at once what kind of book it is. A life of Francis, he says, can be written as secular history, as a devout work, or by an outsider who admires the man and cannot quite follow him. He chooses the third, and writes, he says, for "the ordinary modern man, sympathetic but sceptical". His key is a simple one: that "to this great mystic his religion was not a thing like a theory but a thing like a love-affair". He calls his own work "this thin and scratchy sketch".

It is also a book by someone in love with his subject: the figure in the brown habit, he tells us, stands above the hearth in the room where he writes. That affection is the best thing in it, and it is something to be aware of.
Why it suits a pilgrim

Because the saint is a walker. Chesterton's Francis is, in his phrase, "a man always going somewhere", on the roads of Umbria with a rope for a belt, begging his bread and singing. The book is about leaving, travelling light, courtesy to strangers, gratitude, and the odd joy of having little. It is short, quick and often funny, and it can be read a page at a time. It is also opinionated: Chesterton argues in almost every sentence, and these readings do not try to make him less so.
What the book is, and what it is not
It is a portrait, not Francis's own words.

Everything in the passages is Chesterton's English. The sayings of Francis in it are Chesterton's report of them, and the song of the sun appears only in pieces. This book does not print it whole. Chesterton draws on the early biographers (he names Bonaventura, Celano and the Three Companions) and does not always say which tale comes from where.
It belongs to 1923.

Chesterton writes about other faiths, about the Protestant tradition, and about the Middle Ages and the age before them, which he calls the Dark Ages, with the confidence of a polemicist and the assumptions of his time. His words for Muslims and for the East ("Moslem", "Mahomedan", "oriental") are of that time, and some of his sentences about them read badly now. His second chapter, a sweeping account of the ancient world and the centuries after it, is the most dated part of the book, and we do not use it. We chose passages that do not rest on these assumptions. Where a day comes near one, it says so briefly and moves on.
It retells medieval stories.

Chesterton gathers the miracles into one chapter and says that some of the tales have "the character of fairy stories". This book neither argues for the miracles nor against them. If you want the life as historians now tell it, read a modern life alongside this portrait. They may not always agree with Chesterton.
The edition, the translator and the licence

This is an English original, so there is no translator. We used the text published by Project Gutenberg as ebook number 63084, prepared from scans of an old printing by Hodder and Stoughton, of London and Toronto, in a series called the People's Library. It states no year, so 1923 is the well-known date and not one the file gives. Chesterton died in 1936, and the book is in the public domain. Every passage in these pages was checked against that text, word for word.

The volunteers who prepared the text corrected obvious printer errors, regularised the hyphens and marked italics with underscores. We show those italics as italics, and otherwise changed nothing in the passages, not Chesterton's spelling, his punctuation, or even a
Cæsar

. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. The choice of the nine passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours, and they are original. The passages come from Chapters III to X of the book, with Chapter VI used twice.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.

chapters.title: Day 1. The boast and the turning back

spans.t: What if the road you planned is not the road you are given?
The passage

paras.t: High in the dark house of Assisi Francesco Bernardone slept and dreamed of arms. There came to him in the darkness a vision splendid with swords, patterned after the cross in the Crusading fashion, of spears and shields and helmets hung in a high armoury, all bearing the sacred sign. When he awoke he accepted the dream as a trumpet bidding him to the battlefield, and rushed out to take horse and arms. … As he rode out to war the great gate in the deep wall of Assisi resounded with his last boast, "I shall come back a great prince." A little way along his road his sickness rose again and threw him. It seems highly probable, in the light of his impetuous temper, that he had ridden away long before he was fit to move. And in the darkness of this second and far more desolating interruption, he seems to have had another dream in which a voice said to him, "You have mistaken the meaning of the vision. Return to your own town." And Francis trailed back in his sickness to Assisi, a very dismal and disappointed and perhaps even derided figure, with nothing to do but to wait for what should happen next. It was his first descent into a dark ravine that is called the valley of humiliation, which seemed to him very rocky and desolate, but in which he was afterwards to find many flowers.

cite.t: , Chapter III, Francis the Fighter (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

The first morning of a long walk has a temperature of its own. There is a plan in your pocket: so many kilometres, somewhere to eat at midday, a bed by evening. And there is a body that has not yet agreed to any of it. It is easy to go too fast on a first day, because the road is new and the legs feel full of promise. By the third hour the day begins to say what it thinks. On a road beside the Atlantic, the wind will have an opinion too.

Chesterton's Francis begins in the same place, with a young man and his plan, and Chesterton takes care to show him before anything holy has happened to him. Francis is the son of a cloth merchant in Assisi, popular with everybody, a leader of French fashions, with what Chesterton calls "his guileless swagger as a Troubadour". He throws money about and never quite understands what it is. His mother says, "He is more like a prince than our son." Chesterton insists that at this stage there was no outward sign of anything mystical in him at all. What Francis wanted was to be famous, as a poet and, more often in his thoughts, as a soldier.

So when he dreams of weapons laid up in a high hall, all marked with a cross, he takes it for a summons. The sentence about the gate of Assisi is the one to hear: as he rides out, the great gate "resounded with his last boast". Not a prayer, a boast. Then, a little way down the road, his old sickness throws him. Another dream, or a voice, tells him he has misread the first. He is sent home, "a very dismal and disappointed and perhaps even derided figure".

Say plainly what the passage says. A young man sets out with a story about how it will end. The road corrects the story. And the correction is not even an explanation. He is not told what the dream did mean. He is told only that he was wrong, and to go back and wait for what comes next.

Here is the part worth slowing down for. The last sentence is told from a distance. Francis later found "many flowers" in that valley, Chesterton says, but the one trailing back to Assisi does not know it. To him it is just a bad week. That is how most turnings feel from the inside. And it would be too easy to turn the passage into a promise that every setback hides a gift. It does not say that, and nor will this book. Sometimes a blister is only a blister. Sometimes a closed café is only a closed café. Chesterton can speak of flowers because he knows how the story ends. Nobody on the road today does.

One more thing, calmly. The dream is a dream of its century: swords "patterned after the cross in the Crusading fashion". Francis will turn away from that world, though not at once. In a later chapter Chesterton says his glory would lie not in overthrowing men in battle but in building. We keep the passage because of the road in it, not because of the swords.

So what might it ask of a day of walking? Two small things. The first is to carry the plan lightly. A plan is a good servant on a long walk, and a poor master. If the wind is against you, if your feet say stop, if a village turns out to be shut for lunch and a stranger points you somewhere else, the day may be amending the plan on purpose. The second is to be kind to the self that trails back. A short stage, an early stop, a rest day taken without a lecture: none of these is a failure. Francis did not choose his own descent into the "valley of humiliation" either.

And watch for the boast. Everyone sets out with a small one. It may sound like "I will do thirty kilometres by lunch", or like a picture of yourself arriving at the cathedral. You need not give it up. You need only notice it, and notice what the day does with it.
For the walk

items.t: What have I promised myself about this road, and which part of that promise is a boast? You need not answer aloud. Only be curious about the shape of it.

For the first hour, walk a little slower than feels necessary. Each time you notice yourself speeding up, ask what you are hurrying towards, and then ease off by a step or two. If the answer is simply the end of the day, remember that it will arrive without any help from you.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Somewhere around now, the day you planned and the day you had can be set side by side. They are rarely the same. A shorter stage than you meant, a wrong turn, a hot stretch in the middle of the afternoon, a blister that arrived early: the road has been editing your plan since breakfast. This is a good hour to look at the edits without marking them.

Which did you resist? Think of the moment you most wanted the day to be different. Perhaps it was a long stretch beside the sea with the wind in your face, when you wished yourself anywhere else. Perhaps it was a place you reached later than you had hoped. What did you do with that wish: push on, sulk, laugh, sit down on a wall? There is no right answer, only something worth knowing about yourself.

Then look for the opposite. Was any part of the day better because it did not go to plan? A conversation you would have skipped, a bench you would never have chosen, a small kindness that only turns up when the timetable slips. If nothing comes to mind, that is honest too. Francis in this story gets no consolation on the road home. The consolation, such as it is, is left to a later chapter.

Chesterton's young man also went home looking foolish, and that part is easy to forget. Did you feel foolish today? A wrong turn that a whole café watched you make, a map you read upside down, a pack that came undone at the worst moment. It stings for an hour and then, as a rule, nobody remembers it but you. Francis had a whole town to face. You have, at most, a few strangers who are already thinking about their own feet.

It may also be worth asking about the boast. Not the big one, the small one: the number you were quietly proud of, or the pace you set to impress nobody in particular. Did the road take it from you, or did you hold on? Neither is a fault. A walk of many days has room for a good many corrections, and the early ones are the cheapest.

And a word about tiredness. The first evening of a long walk is a strange one. The body is surprised, the mind is still up in the morning's excitement, and the two do not speak to each other. If you feel low tonight, it may be the plain arithmetic of a first day, not a verdict on the whole walk. Eat something, drink water, wash your feet if you can, and sleep before you decide anything. Tomorrow's road will be a different road with the same legs, and legs are better after a night.
Questions for the end of the day:

items.t: Where did today's road differ from today's plan, and how did I meet the difference?
Was there a moment I walked faster than I needed to, and what was I trying to prove?
What small thing did the slower or unplanned part of the day give me?

spans.t: A short prayer

Bless the plan I made this morning, and the day that changed it. Let me hold both loosely. Take the boast out of my pace. If I was turned round today, let me not mind. Give me rest, and a morning to begin again.

chapters.title: Day 2. Everything that can be called his

spans.t: What would you give back, to be free to go on?
The passage

paras.t: He stood up before them all and said, "Up to this time I have called Pietro Bernardone father, but now I am the servant of God. Not only the money but everything that can be called his I will restore to my father, even the very clothes he has given me." And he rent off all his garments except one; and they saw that that was a hair-shirt. He piled the garments in a heap on the floor and tossed the money on top of them. Then he turned to the bishop, and received his blessing, like one who turns his back on society; and, according to the account, went out as he was into the cold world. Apparently it was literally a cold world at the moment, and snow was on the ground. A curious detail, very deep in its significance, I fancy, is given in the same account of this great crisis in his life. He went out half-naked in his hair-shirt into the winter woods, walking the frozen ground between the frosty trees; a man without a father. He was penniless, he was parentless, he was to all appearance without a trade or a plan or a hope in the world; and as he went under the frosty trees, he burst suddenly into song.

cite.t: , Chapter IV, Francis the Builder (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

Every morning starts with the same small judgement: the pack is lifted, and the shoulders give their verdict. You may find, by the second or third day, that a few things in it have not earned their weight. A third book. A second pair of shoes. A worry that was never packed on purpose and still got in. Walking is a slow audit, and it asks, kilometre by kilometre, what you actually need.

Francis's audit, in Chesterton's telling, was not slow. After the turning back of yesterday there are dark, aimless days, and he spends them praying in a neglected church in Assisi. There he hears a voice say: "Francis, seest thou not that my house is in ruins? Go and restore it for me." He does what he always does, which is to go at once. He sells his horse. Then he sells several bales of his father's cloth, making the sign of the cross over them to show where the money is going. Chesterton does not soften it: "In the coarse conventional language of the uncomprehending world, he stole."

The father is not a villain in this, only a man who finds his stock gone. He locks his son up. Francis hides, and Chesterton calls it "his blackest moment; the whole world had turned over; the whole world was on top of him". Then comes the hearing at the bishop's court, where the bishop, sensibly, tells him to give the money back. And in front of everyone, Francis does something more than that.

Say what the passage says, plainly. Francis does not argue. He gives the money back, and then he goes on, and gives back "everything that can be called his". That includes the clothes his father has given him, and he strips them off in public, down to a rough shirt of hair. He leaves in the snow with nothing: no father, no money, no trade, no plan. And then, Chesterton says, he bursts into song.

The passage is hard, and it is worth saying where. A son shames his father in public, and the sentence "a man without a father" is cold. This is not a model for how to treat anyone's parents. Chesterton is not fair to the father in every line, but he grants, in another chapter, that "there may have been something to be said for Peter Bernardone". Someone reading this may have a father or a mother on their mind this week, perhaps with grief, perhaps with an old quarrel. The passage does not ask anybody to break with their family. It describes one man, one winter, and one very particular call.

What it can ask of the rest of us is smaller and more practical. Look at what you carry that was only handed to you. A title, a reputation, a way of being the sensible one, a set of expectations you never agreed to. On the road much of that may be weightless, because the people beside you do not know your job or your surname. For a few days you are a person with a pack. It is possible to notice, in that lightness, which of the burdens you carry at home were issued by other people, and which you chose.

Notice, too, what comes next in Chesterton's story. After the great renunciation there is no theory. There is work. "He went about by himself collecting stones." And the thought he comes to is a plain one: "The way to build a church is to build it." Letting go is not the end of the day's task. It makes room for the next small task, which is usually to put one foot in front of the other.

One last thing, and it is the odd one. Francis goes out into the cold and sings. The song is not a victory. It is more like the sound a body makes when a weight comes off it. You may know this on a small scale: the first minute after the pack is lowered at a rest stop, when your shoulders do not seem to belong to you. If there is a song in that minute, let it be a short one.
For the walk

items.t: What am I carrying that was handed to me and never chosen? Think of the pack, and then of the rest.

At your next rest, take the pack off and lift it with one hand. Name one thing in it you carry from habit, and one you carry because somebody else expected it. You need not put either down. Only know which is which, and see whether that changes how the straps feel.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The straps come off, and for a few minutes you can feel exactly how heavy the pack was. There is a strange lightness in the shoulders, as if they had been lent to someone else all day and returned. It is the best moment to ask what else was carried today besides the pack.

Some of it may have been very small: a message you were putting off, a conversation you kept replaying, a judgement about how you were doing compared with the people you met. Some of it may have been heavier. A family that is far away, or near, or gone. A job you will go back to. None of it needs to be dropped tonight. The only question is which of it you were carrying out of habit, as a man might hold a coat he has stopped wearing.

Not everything that was handed to you is a burden, and the passage should not be read as if it were. A pair of boots that someone chose for you, a blessing at the door, a recipe, a name: gifts are also things that were given. Francis gave back even the clothes his father had provided. Nobody is asking you to do the same. Keep what was given in love, and keep it with thanks. The question is only which things you are holding by habit, and which by love.

Then there is the song. Francis, in this story, leaves in the snow and sings. Perhaps something in you lifted today for no clear reason: a downhill, a smell of bread, a stranger's laugh from across a square. Perhaps nothing did, and the day was only long. After a hard stretch relief does not always sound like music. Sometimes it is just quiet, and that is also welcome.

Taking off the day's clothes is a small stripping of its own, and it is worth a moment. The sweat-stiff shirt, the socks that have walked all afternoon, the hat that kept the sun off. A wash, a clean shirt, a pair of dry feet. It is an ordinary comfort, and an easy one to overlook. Francis went out into the cold with almost nothing, and the clean shirt tonight is a long way from that, which is a good reason to enjoy it.

Letting go costs energy, and the body does not always know the difference between putting down a worry and picking up a stone. If your head is full tonight, you have not failed at anything. Choose one small thing to be rid of until morning. A wet sock hung up to dry will do. It is surprising how much a small act of putting down can help the larger one.
Questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I carry today that was handed to me and never chosen?
What could I set down for this one night without losing anything I need?
Where, if anywhere, did something in me lift today for no clear reason?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me set down tonight what is not mine to carry. Keep me kind to the people who gave it to me. When the cold comes, let a small song be found in me. If it does not come, let the quiet be enough. Let me sleep light on my shoulders.
Can a gift be enjoyed before it is earned?
The passage

paras.t: It is commonly in a somewhat cynical sense that men have said, "Blessed is he that expecteth nothing, for he shall not be disappointed." It was in a wholly happy and enthusiastic sense that St. Francis said, "Blessed is he who expecteth nothing, for he shall enjoy everything." It was by this deliberate idea of starting from zero, from the dark nothingness of his own deserts, that he did come to enjoy even earthly things as few people have enjoyed them; and they are in themselves the best working example of the idea. For there is no way in which a man can earn a star or deserve a sunset. … The great painter boasted that he mixed all his colours with brains, and the great saint may be said to mix all his thoughts with thanks. All goods look better when they look like gifts.

cite.t: , Chapter V, Le Jongleur de Dieu (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

There is a particular water you drink on a long walk, after hours without it. It is not better water than the water at home. It is only that, for once, you have stopped assuming it. The first mouthful arrives like news. The shade of a single tree does the same, and so does a bench, and so does the moment a stretch of road finally turns towards the place where you will sleep.

Chesterton finds that same feeling at the root of Francis's whole life. In the passage he sets two sayings side by side. The first is the cynic's: "Blessed is he that expecteth nothing, for he shall not be disappointed." It is a way of keeping your guard up. Expect nothing, and nothing can hurt you. Then the saint's version, which changes one clause: "Blessed is he who expecteth nothing, for he shall enjoy everything." Same starting point, opposite road. Where the cynic withdraws, Francis opens his hands.

Chesterton gives the saying to Francis. We have not traced the saying beyond his book, so take it as his report. What is clearer is what he does with it. He says it comes from starting at zero, from "the dark nothingness of his own deserts", and he puts it down in the plainest terms: "there is no way in which a man can earn a star or deserve a sunset". Nobody ever paid for the evening light on the water. The only way to have it is to be given it. And a few lines later he adds a thought which is almost a recipe: "the less a man thinks of himself, the more he thinks of his good luck". It is hard to be amazed while you are busy keeping accounts.

Look at his two examples, too: a star and a sunset. He does not choose a meal or a bed, which can at least be bought. He chooses the things nobody can pay for, or carry off, or put a fence round. The sky is handed to everyone on the same terms, the hurried and the slow, the rich and the penniless.

Notice where this joy comes from in his telling. It does not come from a comfortable life. It comes from the opposite: from the winter woods of yesterday, from a man who has just been stripped of everything he had. A few pages later in the same chapter, Chesterton says it flatly: Francis "certainly was ascetical and he certainly was not gloomy", which is to say that he practised strict self-denial and was not miserable about it. A hard life and a glad one, in the same man, at the same time. That is the oddity this book is going to keep running into.

Put simply, the passage says that joy is easier to find from the bottom than from the middle. When you expect nothing, every small thing arrives as a gift. And all goods, Chesterton adds, look better when they look like gifts.

Now the hard part. "Expecting nothing" is not easy on a bad day. The albergue is full, the café has shut, a blister has opened, the wind has been in your face since morning, and a sentence about enjoying everything may sound like a joke at your expense. It is not a feeling you can order. It is closer to a habit of looking, and habits come slowly. Nor does it mean that you should expect nothing from other people or put up with whatever you are given. A bed that was booked is owed, and you may say so. Francis's phrase is about his own deserts, not anyone else's duties.

And there is a deeper catch for some readers. Chesterton believed that thanks needs somebody to thank. In a sentence we left out of the passage, just before the painter and his colours, Chesterton quotes Rossetti, who said that the worst moment for an atheist is when he is truly thankful and has nobody to thank. You may not share that. You may thank the day, or the sea, or no one at all. The practice does not seem to depend on the address.

In practice it asks something very small: to receive. Not to be grateful on command, not to list ten blessings with your jaw set, but to notice the moment when something arrives that you did not pay for, and to let it arrive. The sun on the water. A path laid by somebody, and kept by somebody else. A stranger's shorthand directions. The first cold mouthful of water.

On the coast there will be plenty of that to receive, and plenty of its opposite: wind, glare, sand in the boots. Both are part of the walk. Francis, in Chesterton's picture, did not enjoy the one by denying the other.
For the walk

items.t: What have I been treating as owed to me today? Start with small things, like a dry path or a free seat, and see how many there are.

Each time you drink water on the road, say a quiet thank you before the second sip. To whom is up to you. See how many times the day gives you the chance, and whether the water tastes any different by evening. If you pass a person who is working to keep the road in order, a gardener, a sweeper, a driver slowing for you, include them.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Food tastes of the day that went before it. A plain bowl of soup after a long road can be a better meal than anything ordered on an easy afternoon, and the reason is the one Francis gives: you had stopped expecting it. Tonight is a good time to look at the day through that single window.

Start with what you did not earn. A cool breeze at the right hour. Someone who pointed the way without being asked. A bench where you did not expect one. The road itself, which somebody laid and somebody keeps. Make the list slowly, in your head, and notice how the list grows once you start. There is no exam at the end.

Then widen the list to people. Somebody made the bed you will sleep in tonight, and somebody will clean the shower you used. Someone grew, cooked or carried the food. A village is a home before it is a stop on a route, and its people give a great deal that never appears on a map. If you can, say a word of thanks before you sleep. A small one, said plainly, goes a long way.

If you passed any water today, a river, a harbour, the open sea, ask whether you really looked at it. Nobody charged admission, and nobody can send a bill for the light on it. A gift of that kind keeps no accounts, which makes it very easy to forget, and very easy to enjoy once you remember. A minute at the window before bed is enough.

Then look at the other side. Was there something you treated as owed today? A seat, a quiet morning, a clean bathroom, a pleasant word from a stranger? It is natural. Most of us walk with an invisible bill for the world. When it goes unpaid, we feel cheated. It is useful, only now and then, to see the bill, and to ask who exactly wrote it.

Gratitude has an awkward feature: it refuses to come on demand. Tiredness is the great enemy of it. When your feet hurt and your head is thick, a list of blessings can feel like a lecture. If that is tonight, put the list down. Do not manufacture a feeling. A single plain "good soup", said once to nobody, is a perfectly respectable thank you. Sleep is a form of thanks as well, and perhaps the most honest one, and the list will still be there in the morning, looking fresher.

Chesterton says the saint "may be said to mix all his thoughts with thanks". Saintliness is not required for a spoonful. One thing, tonight, that was a gift. One word of thanks, aloud or under your breath, to whomever you like.
Three small questions:

items.t: What did I treat as owed to me today, and what was in fact a gift?
What small thing did I enjoy today that I had not expected?
If I could thank one person or thing from today, who or what would it be?

spans.t: A short prayer

For water, for shade, for the road beneath my feet, and for whoever made it, thank you. I did not earn the light on the sea, and I need not. Keep my hands open. Let me sleep thankful, or simply sleep.

chapters.title: Day 4. A stranger on the road

spans.t: Who is the stranger coming up the road, and who are you to the next one?
The passage

paras.t: I mean by the result the real man as he was after his first formative experiences; the man whom men met walking about on the Italian roads in his brown tunic tied with a rope. For that man, saving the grace of God, is the explanation of all that followed; men acted quite differently according to whether they had met him or not. … There is no answer except that Francis Bernardone had happened; and we must try in some sense to see what we should have seen if he had happened to us. In other words, after some groping suggestions about his life from the inside, we must again consider it from the outside; as if he were a stranger coming up the road towards us, along the hills of Umbria, between the olives or the vines.

cite.t: , Chapter VI, The Little Poor Man (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

On a long straight stretch, a boardwalk or a beach or a field track, you can watch someone come towards you for several minutes. At first they are only a shape. Then a hat, a pack, a pace. You cannot tell if they are a pilgrim or a neighbour, and you cannot tell if they are in a good mood. A few seconds before you pass, you both do the same small thing: look up, nod, say
Buen Camino
, and the shape becomes a person for the length of a sentence.

Chesterton asks us to do that with Francis. He has just spent a chapter guessing at Francis from the inside, with the dreams and the cold and the song, and now he stops and says it is time to see the man from the outside. Not the saint in a painting, but a stranger coming up the road "along the hills of Umbria, between the olives or the vines". His reason is odd and bold. If we want to know why a movement swept across Europe, he says, there is no answer except that "Francis Bernardone had happened". And so we should "see what we should have seen if he had happened to us". The people who met him, he adds, "acted quite differently according to whether they had met him or not". The explanation, in other words, is a face under a hood.

What would the face have looked like? Chesterton sketches him elsewhere, and the sketch is not romantic. A small, quick man in a brown tunic tied with a rope. The rope, he says, was snatched up almost at random because it lay nearby, and the clothes were the oldest a peasant could spare. Francis begged for his bread, and chose the worst: "the beggar would eat the best he could get and the saint ate the worst he could get." A traveller from a more comfortable world might have crossed the road.

And yet, says Chesterton, nobody who looked into "those brown burning eyes" came away feeling like one of a crowd. Each man felt that Francis was truly interested in him, in his own life from beginning to end. Chesterton says the only outward form that can carry such a feeling is courtesy. Francis moved among men like "one courtier, moving among a hundred kings". He honoured everyone he met: he loved them, and also respected them. That is a rarer thing than it sounds.

There is a second side to his courtesy, and it is the more surprising one. He asked for things as politely as he gave them. Chesterton says he could beg so confidently for food because he "really did regard every house as the house of a friend". Any pilgrim who has knocked at a door at the end of a day will see how much trust that takes, and how much it puts on the house. It is a compliment to the people who open the door, and also a request.

Put plainly, the passage asks you to picture a poor man on the road and to ask what meeting him did. It claims that something began with an encounter, long before it was an argument or a rule or an order.

The hard part comes from the word "poor". Chesterton is a romantic about Francis, and a pilgrim is in danger of being romantic about poverty, too. A pack, a hostel bunk and a simple supper are a mild, chosen version of it. The people you pass are not all in that position. In another chapter Chesterton himself notes the difference, saying that the churchmen of Francis's day pitied men entering poverty "of their own free will", while the poor of his own day were "daily driven by cold coercion and moved on by the police". It is a fair thing to remember when you walk through a village. Its people are not scenery or lessons. Whatever your pack weighs, you are not living their life.

On an ordinary day it asks you to be a better stranger. Everyone on the road is somebody's stranger. You come up a path towards a farmer, a woman at a gate, a child on a wall, a tired walker sitting on a kerb, and for a moment you are the whole of what they know about pilgrims. Francis's way of doing it was attention, with nothing added. A look that says you are not a statistic. A greeting that treats the other person as somebody who matters.
You will not manage it every time. A hot afternoon is not a good one for courtesy. But it is possible to try once, with one person, and to give them your whole attention for the length of a hello.
For the walk

items.t: If a stranger met me for one minute today, what would they think they had met? Try not to flatter yourself, and not to scold yourself either.

Greet the next few people you pass with your eyes as well as your voice, and give each of them your whole attention for the length of the greeting: no glance at the phone, no thinking of the next sentence. Notice whether anything changes, in them or in you. If a greeting is not returned, let it go without remark.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The people of the day arrive in the mind in no particular order. A face at a counter, a voice calling from a doorway, a walker who passed you twice in the afternoon, a hand lifted from a car window. Some you spoke to, and some you only saw. Tonight you can lay them out for a minute and look at them properly, which you could not do while you were moving.

Then turn it round. For each of those people, you were also somebody coming up the road. What did you look like? Perhaps tired, perhaps glad, perhaps bent over your phone, perhaps humming. There is no need to guess what they thought. It is enough to know that you were part of their day, as they were part of yours, and that a day is partly made of strangers.

If someone asked you for help today, money or a seat or a moment of your time, you will have had your own answer. This reading does not tell you what it should have been. It only invites you to look at it honestly: what you did, and what you felt as you did it. Chesterton's Francis ran after a beggar once, and swore never to refuse a poor man. Most of us cannot keep a vow like that, and it is better to know exactly what we can keep.

Think too about what you gave and what you were given. Directions, perhaps, or a word of warning about a steep stretch, or the loan of a pen. A hand with a gate. On the other side: a seat offered, a ripe fruit, a sentence in a language you half understand. Francis, in Chesterton's picture, was as ready to receive as to give. You may find the exchange on a road is more even than you think.

It may be worth asking where you were not attentive. A moment when somebody spoke and you were already looking past them. A place where you took a photograph of something that was also somebody's front door. Nobody is a saint on a hot afternoon. But Chesterton's point is that courtesy is a form of seeing, and seeing is a habit, and a habit can be started on a Tuesday evening in a quiet room.

And if you walked alone and met almost nobody, that is a day too. You may have been the only stranger for a very long way, and it is worth noticing what that was like. Perhaps you were glad of it. Perhaps you were lonelier than you expected. Either is possible, and neither means the day was wasted.

On tiredness, honestly: the end of a long day is not a time for good manners, and the bunk room does not always get your best. The effort is small. A word of thanks to whoever made the bed. A quiet voice after lights are low. A light turned out early. These are the small hospitalities that make a night shared by strangers easier to bear.
Questions to take to bed:

items.t: Who did I meet today, and did I really look at them?
When did I treat someone as part of the scenery?
What would a stranger have seen if they had met me for one minute today?

spans.t: A short prayer

Make me a gentle stranger. For the faces I met, thank you. For the ones I passed without a look, forgive me. Let someone tomorrow find a welcome in my face, and let me find one in theirs. Bless every house that took a walker in today.
What would it be to meet one thing at a time, and not the whole view?
The passage

paras.t: The phrase about his brotherhood with the sun and moon, and with the water and the fire, occurs of course in his famous poem called the Canticle of the Creatures or the Canticle of the Sun. … It is a supremely characteristic work, and much of St. Francis could be reconstructed from that work alone. … It was not for nothing that he called fire his brother, fierce and gay and strong, and water his sister, pure and clear and inviolate. … A friend of mine said that somebody was the sort of man who apologises to the cat. St. Francis really would have apologised to the cat. When he was about to preach in a wood full of the chatter of birds, he said, with a gentle gesture "Little sisters, if you have now had your say, it is time that I also should be heard." And all the birds were silent; as I for one can very easily believe.

cite.t: , Chapter VI, The Little Poor Man (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

On the coast it is easy to see the sea and nothing else. A strip of grey or blue, a line where it meets the sky, a sound. That is "the view". The gull is part of it, the wave is part of it, the dune is only a texture on the edge. You could walk beside it all day and meet almost none of it.

Chesterton has a sentence that will catch any reader off guard, and it comes in the pages just before the passage. "St. Francis was not a lover of nature." He means something particular. A lover of nature, as he hears the phrase, is someone who likes the world as a pleasant background, a stage set marked "Scene; a wood". For Francis, he says, "nothing was ever in the background". A bird went by him "like an arrow", with a story and a purpose of its own. A bush "could stop him like a brigand". He did not, in Chesterton's phrase, call nature his mother. He "called a particular donkey his brother or a particular sparrow his sister".

That is the point of the passage, and of the song it talks about. The sun and moon, the water and the fire: in Francis's famous poem, the Canticle of the Creatures or of the Sun, they are brothers and sisters, one by one. Chesterton admires the sureness of it. Fire is a brother, "fierce and gay and strong", and water a sister, "pure and clear and inviolate". These are not decorations. They are distinctions, drawn by someone who really looked.

A word about the song itself. This book does not print it. Chesterton gives only pieces, such as the line from his first chapter, "Praised be God for our Sister, Mother Earth, which brings forth varied fruits and grass and glowing flowers". (Earth is a sister and a mother there, so his remark about nature and mothers is about a way of looking, not a count of words.) What we have here is Chesterton's English for Francis's words, and a portrait of the man who sang them. The whole Canticle is easy to find in many translations, and it is short enough to read on a bench.

The passage says this much, simply: Francis treated every creature as someone, and treated someone with courtesy. Chesterton says he would have apologised to the cat. When he came to preach in a wood full of chattering birds, the story goes, he said, "Little sisters, if you have now had your say, it is time that I also should be heard." And the birds, Chesterton says, were silent, "as I for one can very easily believe".

Now the doubt. Plenty of readers will not believe the birds fell silent, and Chesterton does not need them to. A few lines later he calls much of Francis's way with animals "a sort of symbolic joke, a pious pantomime", a way of showing that he "not only loved but reverenced God in all his creatures". The legend is a bow, in other words, and you can take the bow without taking the legend as news. Chesterton's smile in that last clause is part of it.

There is a second difficulty, and it is a practical one on a coast. The elements in the song are not all gentle. Fire is "fierce". The sea is cold and large and does not care who you are. The route guide in the app names wind and sun as the main challenge on this road, and the sun, whom Francis called a brother, can burn. Courtesy to the elements does not mean carelessness with them. Carry water, cover your head and your neck, take shade when it is offered, and rest earlier than your pride suggests. It is a form of manners to arrive in one piece.

On the road it asks for something very small: to choose one thing, and meet it as itself. Not "the sea" but this wave, this one, coming in. Not "birds" but that gull on a post, standing there as if it had been there all morning. It does not need a speech. It needs a minute of attention, and perhaps a quiet nod, as a stranger nods to another.

You may find that a thing looked at in this way changes. It stops being scenery and becomes an event. That is all Chesterton is claiming for Francis: not that he loved the world in general, but that he met it in particular, which is harder and, for a walker, a good deal more interesting.
For the walk

items.t: What is one thing on this road that I could look at today as if it were not scenery?

Choose one living thing, a gull, a tree, a lizard on a wall, a dog on a doorstep that you watch from a respectful distance, and give it a full minute of attention. If you like, greet it by a name of your own making. It is a courtesy, not a belief, and no one is checking. Do not touch wild creatures, and keep away from animals you do not know.

spans.t: At the end of the day
By evening there is salt on your skin and sand in places you did not know had places. It is a good moment to ask what, out of the whole day's view, you actually met.

Perhaps nothing, and the day went by as a long stretch of "the view". That is the usual way, and there is no reproach in it. Or perhaps one thing stopped you: a bird, a gust, a trick of the light on wet sand, a dog that looked at you and decided you were fine. Go back to it for a moment. What was it like? What did it do?

Water and fire are good guides for the evening. Water: what did it do for you today? The first drink, a wash at the end, the sound of the sea, the cold of a tap. Fire: the heat of the sun on your neck, a stove, a candle, a warm cup in the hands. In the pages after the passage, Chesterton tells how, near the end of his life, when a red-hot iron was about to be brought close to Francis's failing eyes, he rose and spoke to the fire: "Brother Fire, God made you beautiful and strong and useful; I pray you be courteous with me." It is a startling moment, and Chesterton calls it a masterpiece of "the art of life". It is also a reminder that courtesy to the world does not require the world to be kind. It is something you offer, whatever comes.

The one element left out of the list is earth, the ground itself, which Francis's song calls both a sister and a mother. Your feet will have a good deal to say about it tonight. Sand that slides, boards that ring, cobbles that bruise, a hard shoulder of tarmac, a soft patch of grass that was a gift. Every kind of ground speaks differently to the sole of a foot. It held you up for hours and asked for nothing. That is worth a thought before the shoes come off, and perhaps a quiet word of thanks as you take them off.

If today's weather was harsh, wind, glare or a long grey drizzle, you could try the same attitude: not an enemy, and not a friend, but something with a character, which you can meet with manners. Your sunburn, if you have one, is not a moral failure. Take care of it, and be glad of the sun at the same time.

Tiredness flattens all of this. After a long day the mind goes grey, and a thing like a gull ceases to be interesting. Do not try to be moved. If you can manage one clear minute at the window, with whatever is outside it, that is plenty.
Questions for the last light:

items.t: What one thing did I truly meet today, and not merely pass?
Where did I speak to something, a bird, a dog, the wind, even as a joke, with some courtesy?
What in today's weather was hard, and could I take it as a character and not an enemy?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the sun and the wind and the water, for the gull on the post, and the sand in my shoes, thank you. Teach me to meet each thing as itself. Let tomorrow's wind be gentle with me, and let me be gentle with what I meet. Keep me from burns and blisters, and let the night be calm.

chapters.title: Day 6. Nothing to hold him by

spans.t: What can the world catch you by?
The passage

paras.t: The good Bishop of Assisi expressed a sort of horror at the hard life which the Little Brothers lived at the Portiuncula, without comforts, without possessions, eating anything they could get and sleeping anyhow on the ground. St. Francis answered him with that curious and almost stunning shrewdness which the unworldly can sometimes wield like a club of stone. He said, "If we had any possessions, we should need weapons and laws to defend them." That sentence is the clue to the whole policy that he pursued. … There was nothing that the world could hold them by; for the world catches us mostly by the fringes of our garments, the futile externals of our lives. … A man had to be thin to pass always through the bars and out of the cage; he had to travel light in order to ride so fast and so far. … You could not put his head in a halter without the risk of putting it in a halo.

cite.t: , Chapter VII, The Three Orders (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

Watch how a very small thing can hold a whole afternoon. A phone at five per cent. A sandal strap that has begun to rub. The time on a clock that says you are slower than you meant to be. None of these is large. Together they decide your mood for hours, and the mood decides how you see everything else. The world, as Chesterton puts it in this passage, "catches us mostly by the fringes of our garments".

The passage comes from the moment when Francis's little band is no longer only a few friends. First there was Bernard, a wealthy townsman, and Peter, a churchman, who followed Francis when most people, Chesterton guesses, took him for a madman. Then a man named Egidio, apparently a poor workman, made it four. Chesterton calls them the Little Brothers, and he says that is closer to the name Francis used than "Friars Minor". They lived at a small church called the Portiuncula, with no comforts, no property, and anything they could get to eat. The bishop of Assisi, a kind man, was horrified. Francis answered with a sentence Chesterton thinks says it all: "If we had any possessions, we should need weapons and laws to defend them."

It is a plain argument, and a practical one. What you own, you must protect. What you must protect, you will sooner or later fight over. A man with nothing to defend is hard to threaten. You could not starve a man who was already fasting, Chesterton says, or ruin one who was already a beggar. The brothers were meant to be like "little fishes who could go freely in and out of that net", and they could do it because there was nothing to snag. "A man had to be thin to pass always through the bars and out of the cage; he had to travel light in order to ride so fast and so far." The last line of the passage is the best of them: you could not put his head in a halter without risking a halo.

In short, the passage makes poverty a freedom instead of a sorrow. The Little Brothers were not poor because they disliked the world. They were poor so that they could go anywhere, among any kind of people, and not be held. One of the later Franciscans, Chesterton says, put it in a line: "A monk should own nothing but his harp." Keep the song, and lose the luggage.

Now say where it is hard. First, it is a vocation and not a rule for everyone. Chesterton says so himself: "there is a sense in which the ordinary man cannot be free from the world; or rather ought not to be free from the world." A parent with a child cannot travel light. A person caring for someone at home cannot, either. Those are ties to be proud of. Francis did not want all of Italy on the road. Chesterton says he foreshadowed a Third Order for people who stayed in their homes, meant to help them "to be ordinary with an extraordinary exultation". The lightness was for a few, and the spirit of it for everyone else.

Second, there is a trap in admiring the whole thing from a walker's point of view. A pilgrim's lightness is borrowed. The pack comes off at the end of the walk and the house, the shelves and the diary come back. To feel light for a week or two is not the same as to live light for life, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Francis chose it, and in Chesterton's telling never turned back. You are allowed to simply enjoy the lightness for what it is.
One more detail shows how much the rule mattered. Chesterton says Francis "was only once seen angry; and that was when there was talk of an exception to the rule".

What it asks of you, on an ordinary day, is not a vow. It asks only that you find your own fringes: the small thing the world is using to hold you by the sleeve. A battery, a pace, a comparison with the walker ahead, a hunger that is bigger in the mind than in the stomach. Once you can name it, it often loosens. You do not have to throw it away. You only have to see that it is a fringe, and not the garment.
For the walk

items.t: What is holding my mood by the sleeve right now? Look for the small, specific thing, not the large one.

Check the route when you need to, and then put the phone away for an hour. Let your hands be empty for part of it, and swing your arms a little. Notice what you reach for, and what that tells you. If you find you cannot manage an hour, take twenty minutes, and be pleased with those.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The pack comes open on the bed, and the whole of your life for the week fits across a bunk. Spare shirt, socks, a little soap, the things for your feet, a charger, a book you have not opened, perhaps a keepsake. It always looks smaller laid out than it felt on the shoulders. It is a good picture to keep. Most of what you needed today was in it, and most of what held you up was not.

Go back through the day for the fringes. Where did the world catch you? Perhaps in the ache of one foot, which became the whole day. Perhaps in a glance at the time, or a message that did not come, or a brief unkind sentence you rehearsed about someone. It is worth being gentle about this. Everyone has handles. The point is not to be free of all of them. It is to know a few by name.

There is another half of Chesterton's story that suits the evening. The Little Brothers were light, but they were never alone. A little later in the same chapter, he tells of a young friar who had got it into his head that Francis despised him. Francis went straight up to the young man, and said: "Be not troubled in your thoughts for you are dear to me". Then he asked him to come in confidence whenever he liked. That is the other side of travelling light: you must lean on someone.

So think of the company of the day. A walker who shared water, a joke in a queue, a host who found you a bed, a friend who sent a word from home. Which of them made the road lighter? You may not have told them. A word tonight, or tomorrow, costs nothing and is the one thing that cannot be left in the pack.

Chesterton's monk was allowed one possession, a harp. If you could keep one thing that has no use at all, something for the song and not the luggage, what would it be? A tune you hum without noticing, a habit of looking up at birds, a person you think of when you are tired. It does not have to be grand. It only has to be yours, and light enough to carry.
And if you walked alone and felt lonely at the thought of lightness, that is honest, and understandable. Light and lonely are not the same, but they can feel alike at nine in the evening.

In the evening the mind tends to hold on tighter than it did in the morning. Tired people cling, to a message, to tomorrow's plan, to the exact rank of their aches. If you notice that, you need not argue with it. Put the pack where you can reach it in the dark, set one alarm, and let the rest go until the light comes.
Questions for the bunk:

items.t: What was holding my mood by the sleeve today?
What do I really need from what I carry, and what is only fringe?
Who made today's road lighter, and have I told them?

spans.t: A short prayer
Teach me to travel light. Let nothing small hold me by the sleeve tomorrow. Thank you for the people who made the road shorter. Keep me free and keep me kind. Give me a bed, and give me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 7. What may never be known

spans.t: How do you walk beside something you cannot explain?
The passage

paras.t: What it was exactly that happened there may never be known. The matter has been, I believe, a subject of dispute among the most devout students of the saintly life as well as between such students and others of the more secular sort. It may be that St. Francis never spoke to a soul on the subject; it would be highly characteristic, and it is certain in any case that he said very little; I think he is only alleged to have spoken of it to one man. … Finally after some fashion the apocalypse faded from the sky and the agony within subsided; and silence and the natural air filled the morning twilight and settled slowly in the purple chasms and cleft abysses of the Apennines. The head of the solitary sank, amid all that relaxation and quiet in which time can drift by with the sense of something ended and complete; and as he stared downwards, he saw the marks of nails in his own hands.

cite.t: , Chapter VIII, The Mirror of Christ (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

Some mornings by the sea the fog rubs out the horizon. The road is where it was, and the next marker is there somewhere, but the world has shrunk to the few paces ahead. There is a particular quiet in that, and also a small unease. You are used to knowing what is coming. Today you walk beside a great deal that you cannot see, and you go on anyway.

Francis's story has a stretch of that sort of fog, and Chesterton, to his credit, does not try to clear it. This day's passage comes at the end of a long chapter, so a few words of background are needed first.

The chapter follows Francis's wish to be as like Christ as he could. In Chesterton's telling that wish took him across the sea. His first attempt, a sail for the East, has a comic edge. He saw a boat, threw himself into it without waiting for introductions or bargains, "becoming the Patron Saint of Stowaways", and lay "like lumber among the cargo". The voyage turned out "unfortunate and erratic" and ended with a return to Italy. A later voyage got further. He reached the camp of the Crusaders outside the city of Damietta, went on alone to speak with the Sultan, and came back, Chesterton says, "as freely as he came". The aim, as Chesterton puts it, was to end the Crusades "by conversion and not by conquest". The whole effort broke off short. "Men liked him too much for himself to let him die for his faith," Chesterton writes, and he calls the whole venture the "beginnings of a great bridge that might have united East and West".

Here the book has to say something plainly. Chesterton writes about Islam and about "the East" in the language of 1923, and with a confidence we do not share. Some of his sentences in this chapter read badly now. We have left them out of the passage and have not tried to defend them. One thing in his account holds up without them: a man went from one camp of a war to the other, to talk, and went alone.

Then Francis turned towards the mountains. A gentleman with lands in Tuscany gave him a mountain, "a thing somewhat unique among the gifts of the world", and he used it as a place for prayer. The mountain is Alverno. And here is the sentence this day is built on: "What it was exactly that happened there may never be known."

In the stretch we have left out, Chesterton describes what Francis is said to have seen: a winged figure filling the sky, like a seraph spread out in the shape of a cross, in pain. At the end of the passage the vision is gone, the morning is quiet, and Francis looks down and sees "the marks of nails in his own hands". These are what Christians call the stigmata, wounds like those of the crucified Christ. Chesterton takes the account as true. He says the one thin report that has come down "reads very like the report of something real".

You may take the story as a miracle, or as a mystery, or as a tale you cannot judge. This book does not argue for or against it. What it can say is what the passage does: Chesterton does not pretend to know more than he does. He gives the dispute, the silence, and the quiet air over the Apennines, and he stops.

Now say where it is hard. In this chapter Chesterton tells us that a refrain ran through Francis's days: "I have not suffered enough; I have not sacrificed enough." He "wandered about the valleys of the world looking for the hill that has the outline of a skull." Nothing here asks you to want pain. A blister is not a sacrifice to be hoarded, and an aching knee is not a gift to be sought. If you are walking with pain today, your own or someone else's, this reading asks only that you be gentle.

What can it ask of an ordinary day, then? Something much smaller than a vision: to let one thing stay unexplained. You may meet a thing like that on any long walk. A feeling that arrives on a hill and does not fit anywhere. A grief that is not for any reason you can name. A joy with no cause. The habit of the mind is to explain it at once, to file it, to turn it into a sentence for a post. Chesterton's habit, here, is to wait. Where something "may never be known", there is still a perfectly good place to stand.
For the walk

items.t: What is there in my life that I cannot explain, and could I carry it for one day without explaining it?

At some point in the morning, stop for one minute. Let your hands hang. Listen to the farthest sound you can find, and the nearest. Do not name anything. When the minute is over, walk on without telling anyone what it was.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The best conversations of the day may have been the ones without an answer. A sentence at a table that nobody finished. A question a stranger asked about why you were walking, which you answered one way at lunch and another way at supper. Evening is a good hour to notice how many things go unexplained, and how well you got on without it.

Chesterton's own honesty is worth borrowing. He says that what happened on the mountain "may never be known", and a few sentences later that, "to me personally", the one report that has come down "reads very like the report of something real". It is possible to hold both. A hunch and a doubt can share a bench. The day's strangest moment need not be resolved before you sleep. Perhaps it will keep.

It is worth remembering that the same chapter has a joke in it. A saint who sets out for the other end of the sea by lying like lumber in somebody else's cargo is allowed to make you smile, and Chesterton clearly meant him to. Awe and humour keep company more often than people expect. If something today made you laugh at yourself, a missed turn, a pack dropped in front of an audience, you may have been closer to Francis than you thought.

If there was pain in the day, a foot, a back, a grief that came up in a quiet hour, you carried it well enough to get here. It does not have to be turned into a lesson. A hot shower, if there is one, and a plain meal are a respectable way of answering it. If the pain is worse than usual, or does not ease, or worries you, see a doctor, or ask your host where to find one. The standard European emergency number is 112. There is no prize for walking on a problem.

And then the small thing about silence. The passage ends in it: "silence and the natural air filled the morning twilight". You may find the evening has a silence of its own, after the stove and the voices and the last tap running. If you can, give it one minute before you reach for the phone. There is nothing in it to fix.

It may help to notice, too, what you left unsaid today. A word held back at a table, a name you did not look up, a feeling you let pass without a comment. Not all silence is a failure of nerve. Some of it is courtesy, and some of it is simply the right size for the thing.
A tired mind wants every question answered so that it can stop. Tonight, let some of them stay on the table. They will still be there in the morning, and a rested mind is a better judge of them.
Questions to leave open:

items.t: What did I try to explain today that might have been better left alone?
What can I carry for a while without understanding it?
Where did I find quiet today, even for a minute?

spans.t: A short prayer

For what I cannot explain, give me patience. Let me hold it gently and not rush it into words. Where there is pain in me or near me tonight, ease it. Give me a quiet that is not empty, and let that be enough.
What is it to lie down at the end?
The passage

paras.t: He who had become a vagabond for the sake of a vision, he who had denied himself all sense of place and possession, he whose whole gospel and glory it was to be homeless, received like a Parthian shot from nature, the sting of the sense of home. He also had his

, his sickness of the spire; though his spire was higher than ours. "Never," he cried with the sudden energy of strong spirits in death, "never give up this place. If you would go anywhere or make any pilgrimage, return always to your home; for this is the holy house of God." … After he had taken farewell of some of his nearest and especially some of his oldest friends, he was lifted at his own request off his own rude bed and laid on the bare ground; as some say clad only in a hair-shirt, as he had first gone forth into the wintry woods from the presence of his father. It was the final assertion of his great fixed idea; of praise and thanks springing to their most towering height out of nakedness and nothing. … But at least in the passages and porches of the Portiuncula there was a sudden stillness, where all the brown figures stood like bronze statues; for the stopping of the great heart that had not broken till it held the world.

cite.t: , Chapter IX, Miracles and Death (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

There comes a point on most long afternoons when you would give a good deal to lie flat on the ground. Not to sleep. Only to be held up by something that asks nothing of you. The back lets go, the shoulders drop, the sky is very large. For a minute the whole business of getting somewhere is suspended, and the earth does the work.

Chesterton brings his story of Francis to rest in that posture. Today's passage is the last scene of a life, and it is told gently. Francis is dying. He is not yet fifty, Chesterton says, and worn out. He has been carried from place to place, and then, as the procession comes near Assisi, something lifts him. He sees "afar off on the Assisian hill" the pillars of the Portiuncula, the small church where his brotherhood began. And the man who made homelessness his glory, Chesterton says, receives "like a Parthian shot from nature, the sting of the sense of home". He calls it a sickness of the spire, a homesickness that fastens on a church tower, and adds that Francis's spire was higher than ours.

What Francis says next is the line a pilgrim reader will stop at: "If you would go anywhere or make any pilgrimage, return always to your home; for this is the holy house of God." Say it carefully. He is speaking of the Portiuncula, which Chesterton calls his home. He is not telling anybody to go back to their own front door. Chesterton finds the whole moment "profoundly pathetic, and full of great problems" (he means moving, not feeble): a man who spent his life leaving feels, at the very end, the pull of a place.

Then he is lifted from his bed and laid, at his own request, on the bare ground. Chesterton says it was "the final assertion of his great fixed idea; of praise and thanks springing to their most towering height out of nakedness and nothing". The idea is the one you met in the winter woods on the second day, and it comes round again. He ends as he began: with nothing, and with thanks.

The last stretch of the passage is quiet. The brothers stand round him in their brown habits, and in "a sudden stillness" they look like bronze statues. The great heart stops. It was a heart, Chesterton says in the sentence that closes the scene, "that had not broken till it held the world".

The song comes into this, though not in these lines. In the first chapter Chesterton remarks that the famous song of praise, the one that names the sun and the earth, ends almost with the words "Praised be God for our Sister, the death of the body." So the song's closing praise goes to death, and calls it a sister. It is one of the strangest and most beautiful things in the story, and it should not be tidied.

It also has to be said, honestly, that for many people death is not a sister. It is a loss, and some who walk the Camino carry it with them. Chesterton does not pretend otherwise on this page. He writes of the long day wearing on, and of how "that great darkness descended in which we all lost a friend". A reader who has lost someone is not asked to feel brotherly about it today. Nobody should be hurried into praise.

What this asks of a day is almost nothing grand. A day, too, ends, and a day can be ended well or badly. There is a plain wisdom in lying down at the end of it with something said: a thanks, a forgiveness, a task honestly left for tomorrow. Francis did it on the largest scale there is. You can do it on a bunk. Nothing in the passage requires you to be a saint. It asks only that you notice that the ground holds you, and that you are allowed to be held.

And the other line, the one about home. If you are near the end of your own walk, or reading this at home after one, "return always to your home" may sound comforting or may not. Homes are complicated. For some of us the word means a table with people at it, and for others a flat with a quiet hall. Francis's home was a small church and a group of friends. What is yours?
For the walk

items.t: What would I want to have said thank you for before this day is over?

The next time you sit down, on a bench or a wall or the grass, put your hand flat on whatever is holding you. If the ground is dry and the place is safe, take your weight off your feet for three slow breaths. Feel what carries you, and let it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Lying down is the oldest way of ending a day, and tonight you will do it without thinking. The body is flat, the eyes close, and for a few minutes you are held up by a mattress or a bunk or a floor, much as Francis was held up by the ground. It is worth noticing how completely the body trusts it.

This is also the hour to ask what has finished today. A day does not come back. The stage you walked is behind you, the people you met are scattered, the weather has moved on. Is there anything you would like to say before it closes? A thank you not yet spoken, a small sorry, a message that has been waiting since lunchtime. It is not a will, and nothing here is final. It is only the small custom of leaving a day tidy.

Francis, in Chesterton's picture, praised from nakedness and nothing. Tonight's version is far smaller, and also real. Look at what you actually have in the room: a bed, a blanket, a cup of water, shoes lined up by the wall, a pack with everything you need. It is not nothing, and it is not much. It is a fair place to say thank you from, and the thanks need not be long. "Enough" is a whole sentence.

Some people walk the Way in grief for someone who has died. If that is you, tonight may be heavy, and the passage may have been hard to read. You need not make anything of it. The prayer below can be said for them, with or without belief. If there is a name you would like to say aloud, the room is probably quiet enough.

And a thought about home, since the passage raised it. Who knows where you are tonight, and who is thinking of you? Not everyone has someone, and it is as well to say so. If you do, a short message might do both of you good. If you do not, you may want to be that person for somebody else.

In the evening the body asks for very little, and it is wise to listen: water, something to eat, feet up if there is a way. The heaviest thoughts are often only tired thoughts, and they look different in the morning. If one of them does not, it is a thought to share with someone, not to carry alone. And if sleep will not come, lie still anyway. Lying quietly with the eyes closed and the breathing slow is also a kind of rest, and it counts.
Questions for lying down:

items.t: What would I like to have said thank you for before this day ends?
Is there anyone I am carrying with me on this walk, living or gone, and what would I say to them tonight?
What does "home" mean to me this evening: a place I am returning to, or one I am leaving?

spans.t: A short prayer

For this day, now finished, thank you. For the ground that held me up, thank you. Let me lie down without fear and wake without hurry. For those I carry with me, living and gone, give peace. Let me be at home tonight, wherever I am.
How do you go on, when the road has taught you what it can?
The passage

paras.t: It is perhaps the chief suggestion of this book that St. Francis walked the world like the Pardon of God. I mean that his appearance marked the moment when men could be reconciled not only to God but to nature and, most difficult of all, to themselves. … He was not a mere eccentric because he was always turning towards the centre and heart of the maze; he took the queerest and most zigzag short cuts through the wood, but he was always going home. … For that is the full and final spirit in which we should turn to St. Francis; in the spirit of thanks for what he has done. He was above all things a great giver; and he cared chiefly for the best kind of giving which is called thanksgiving.

cite.t: , Chapter X, The Testament of St. Francis (English original, 1923)

spans.t: Reflection

A coast road rarely goes straight. It follows the edge of the land, and the edge of the land is a long argument between rock and water: a boardwalk that ends at an estuary, a detour round a headland, a stretch inland because the shore has given up. Anyone who has walked such a road knows the odd sense of progress it gives. You are not going the shortest way. You are going the way the ground allows, and you are, all the same, getting there.

Chesterton's last chapter is about that same kind of progress. He steps back from the story and asks what Francis left. The first half of the chapter is an argument about the quarrels that followed his death, and about whether the Popes were right to restrain the stricter Franciscans. Chesterton is a partisan in it, and sure of himself, and we have left it out. The passage comes from the later pages, where he tries to say what the whole story was for.

It begins with a bold phrase: "St. Francis walked the world like the Pardon of God." By "pardon" he means something like a fresh start. A little later he says it was Francis's "whole function to tell men to start afresh". His appearance, he says, marked the moment when men could be reconciled to God, to nature and, "most difficult of all, to themselves". A reader who does not share his faith may hear the word "pardon" as a plain one: a door left open, a new page.

Look at the last item on that list. Reconciled to themselves. It is the hardest of the three, and there is a reason it comes last. A long walk shows you a good deal. How fast you go and how soon you tire. What you do with an empty stomach. How you talk to strangers, and to yourself, when nobody is watching. Some of that you may like, and some of it you may not. To be reconciled with it is to stop waiting for a different person to do the walking. You are the one with the pack, and you are doing it.
